Employees on your team are watching you for cues on how they should behave. The behaviors a CEO models, for example, will trickle down to her team and further until those behaviors are replicated throughout the organization. Whether you want to increase reporting or speaking up behaviors about patient safety or develop a stronger learning culture for safety, these behaviors must first be modeled by leadership.  

### Why is it important?

According to the Joint Commission's 2017 article, "The essential role of leadership in developing a safety culture," CEO's and all leaders must adopt and model appropriate behaviors and champion efforts to eradicate intimidating behaviors.  **Several recommendations for modeling your commitment to safety are below:**

- **Model Personal Accountability for Patient Safety**  
If you've made a recent or past mistake involving patient safety, share this with your team and how the situation was ultimately handled. Modeling this type of transparency will let your team know that their input about patient safety is valued and should encourage more reporting behaviors. According to the Joint Commission's 2018 report "Developing a reporting culture: Learning from close calls and hazardous conditions," It's important for leaders to be strong role models and be among the first to raise their own hands and say "I made a mistake." Staff and unit managers will start to model this accountability when they see the engagement of leadership.

- **Conduct Leadership WalkRoundsâ„¢ to Model your Commitment to Patient Safety**  
According to the Institute of Healthcare Improvement, these should be conducted by senior leaders at least once a week without cancellations to help connect senior leaders and those team members working at the point of care.  A guide recommended by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement is located [here](http://www.ihi.org/resources/Pages/Tools/PatientSafetyLeadershipWalkRounds.aspx). These conversations between senior leaders and front-line employees will demonstrate the importance of patient safety and the value of safety reporting and suggestions to improve safety.    

- **Get Involved in Daily Huddles or Safety Briefings**  
Your involvement in these huddles will demonstrate how much you value patient safety - even if you don't say a word in the huddle. If you are a senior leader, attend the unit huddles two levels down within the organization a few times per month. If you can't attend all the safety huddles held by your team, make sure to at least be a consistent presence at these weekly.   

- **Never Engage in Disruptive Behaviors and Hold Those who do Accountable**  
While they acknowledge that there is no standard definition of disruptive behavior, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) reports that most authorities include any behavior that shows disrespect for others, or any interpersonal interaction that impedes the delivery of patient care. Disruptive behavior negatively impacts a culture of patient safety. When teammates feel that their input or concerns about patient safety could be belittled by a leader, colleague, or physician, they're less likely to speak up. Leaders must model their commitment to patient safety by adopting a "zero tolerance" policy towards disruptive behavior, regardless of employee level.    

#### Case Studies of Leadership Safety Modeling

Adventist Hinsdale Hospital improved its error and near-miss reporting and decreased events causing harm after senior leader communication, access and visibility increased. Senior leaders began rounding regularly on all three shifts to assess and respond to safety concerns, and they began advocating for stopping the line, implementing the chain of command, and other staff driven safety interventions. Senior leaders also regularly attended staff meetings, worked with nurses side by side, and publicized decisions made for safety purposes in multiple forums.
